title: Diagnosing Diabetes: Glucose Cut-offs and When HbA1c Lies
summary: Climb three diagnostic ladders — fasting glucose, 2-hour OGTT and HbA1c — watch glucose stick to a red cell over its lifetime, and learn why transfusion or bleeding makes HbA1c untrustworthy.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 17 Hit 1 (core: diagnostic cut-offs), Hits 2 and 10, Traps 1 and 5 and the Figure 17 memory anchor. All cut-offs are checked against the ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 2, which also adds the two-abnormal-results rule and the list of conditions that make HbA1c unreliable.

objectives: State the diagnostic and prediabetes cut-offs for fasting glucose, 2-hour OGTT and HbA1c.
Explain what HbA1c reflects and when it cannot be used for diagnosis.
Apply the confirmation rule and the one-step gestational-diabetes criteria.

scenes.title: Three numbers that mean “diabetes”
scenes.altText: Three lab cards appear: a fasting glucose, a 2-hour glucose after a sugar drink, and an HbA1c. A fourth patient card shows HbA1c 6.9% — but the patient was transfused last week. The cartoon scientist hesitates.

cues.text: The lab can diagnose diabetes three main ways: a fasting glucose, a glucose two hours after a sugar drink, or an HbA1c.
Each has a cut-off. Above it, the result counts toward a diagnosis.
But here is a patient with an HbA1c of 6.9 percent — above the line — who had a blood transfusion last week. Can we trust it?

props.label: HbA1c 6.9% · transfused last week → trust it?

scenes.title: The three ladders
scenes.altText: Three vertical ladders with three bands each — normal (bottom), prediabetes (middle), diabetes (top). Fasting plasma glucose: < 100 / 100–125 / ≥ 126 mg/dL. 2-hour 75-g OGTT: < 140 / 140–199 / ≥ 200 mg/dL. HbA1c: < 5.7 / 5.7–6.4 / ≥ 6.5%. A marker slides up each ladder as the numbers are read.

cues.text: Picture three ladders. Each has three rungs: normal at the bottom, prediabetes in the middle, diabetes at the top.
Fasting plasma glucose: under 100 is normal, 100 to 125 is prediabetes, and 126 or higher counts toward diabetes.
Two hours after a 75-gram sugar drink: under 140 is normal, 140 to 199 is prediabetes, and 200 or higher counts toward diabetes.
HbA1c: under 5.7 percent is normal, 5.7 to 6.4 is prediabetes, and 6.5 or higher counts toward diabetes.
One more route: a random glucose of 200 or more — but only in a patient with classic symptoms like heavy thirst and urination.

props.label: Random ≥ 200 mg/dL counts only WITH classic symptoms

scenes.title: What HbA1c really measures
scenes.altText: A red cell drifts through glucose-rich plasma; glucose tokens stick to it one by one over its roughly 120-day life, and a counter shows “days 0 → 120”. Then the scene changes: transfused fresh cells and young cells after bleeding carry few glucose tokens, so the average drops even though blood glucose did not change. A card lists conditions where ADA says to use plasma glucose instead: pregnancy, G6PD deficiency, HIV, and anything that changes red-cell turnover (bleeding, transfusion, hemolysis). Alternatives: fructosamine and glycated albumin.

cues.text: Glucose slowly sticks to hemoglobin inside red cells. The higher the blood sugar, the more sticks.
A red cell lives about 120 days, so HbA1c reflects average glucose over the past few months.
Now change the cells, not the sugar. Fresh transfused cells, or young cells made after bleeding or hemolysis, have had little time to collect glucose.
So the HbA1c no longer matches the true average glucose. ADA says to use plasma glucose criteria in pregnancy, G6PD deficiency, HIV and conditions that change red-cell turnover.
When HbA1c can’t be trusted for monitoring, labs can measure fructosamine or glycated albumin instead.

props.text: Fresh / young cell: little glucose yet

props.title: Use plasma glucose instead (ADA)
lines: Changed red-cell turnover: bleeding, transfusion, hemolysis

scenes.title: In the lab: confirm, and pregnancy rules
scenes.altText: A “two abnormal results” rule: two result cards (fasting 131 and HbA1c 6.7%) click together into “Diabetes confirmed”; one card alone shows “repeat or add a second test”. Then a pregnancy panel: 75-g OGTT at 24–28 weeks with three time points — fasting ≥ 92, 1 hour ≥ 180, 2 hours ≥ 153 mg/dL — and the rule “any one value met or exceeded = gestational diabetes”.

cues.text: One high result is not enough. Unless hyperglycemia is unequivocal, ADA requires two abnormal results — from the same sample or from two different times.
For example, a fasting glucose of 131 plus an HbA1c of 6.7 percent on the same visit confirms diabetes.
Pregnancy has its own test. The one-step approach gives a 75-gram glucose drink at 24 to 28 weeks and measures glucose fasting, at 1 hour and at 2 hours.
The cut-offs are lower: fasting 92, 1 hour 180, 2 hours 153 milligrams per decilitre.
And here, any ONE value at or above its cut-off diagnoses gestational diabetes.

props.text: One result alone → repeat or add a second test

props.title: Pregnancy: one-step 75-g OGTT at 24–28 weeks
lines: Glucose fasting, at 1 h and at 2 h

props.label: ANY one value met or exceeded = GDM

scenes.title: Two classic traps
scenes.altText: Trap card: “HbA1c 6.9% after a transfusion = diabetes” is crossed out → “Red-cell turnover changed: use plasma glucose criteria.” Trap card: “Random glucose 215 in a patient with no symptoms = diabetes” is crossed out → “Random ≥ 200 counts only with classic symptoms; otherwise confirm with fasting glucose, OGTT or HbA1c.”

cues.text: Trap one: an HbA1c of 6.9 percent after a transfusion, bleeding or hemolysis. It is above 6.5, but the red cells changed, so the number can’t be trusted. Use plasma glucose.
Trap two: a random glucose of 215 in someone with no symptoms. A random glucose of 200 or more diagnoses diabetes only with classic symptoms. Otherwise, confirm with another test.
And remember pregnancy is different: lower cut-offs, and any single value is enough.

props.title: ✗ “HbA1c 6.9% after transfusion = diabetes.”
lines: ✓ Red-cell turnover changed → use plasma glucose

props.title: ✗ “Random 215, no symptoms = diabetes.”
lines: ✓ Random ≥ 200 counts only with classic symptoms

scenes.altText: Memory aid: a door numbered 126 (fasting), a door numbered 200 (two hours after the drink, or random with symptoms), and a door numbered 6.5 (HbA1c). A pregnant figure walks through smaller doors labelled 92 · 180 · 153. A card lists where the aid breaks down.

cues.text: Memory aid: three doors — 126 fasting, 200 after the drink, 6.5 on the cells. Walk through any door twice, or two doors once each, and it’s diabetes.
Pregnancy uses smaller doors: 92, 180, 153 — and one door is enough.
Where it breaks: the 6.5 door is locked when red-cell turnover changes, and the random-200 door opens only with symptoms. Outside pregnancy, you still need a second abnormal result.

props.title: Where it breaks
lines: 6.5 fails when red-cell turnover changes · random 200 needs symptoms · confirm with a second result

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Three tokens: “Fasting ≥ 126 · 2-h ≥ 200 · HbA1c ≥ 6.5% (confirm)”, “HbA1c unreliable when red-cell turnover changes”, “GDM: 92 / 180 / 153 — any one”.

cues.text: Diabetes is diagnosed by a fasting glucose of 126 or more, a 2-hour OGTT of 200 or more, or an HbA1c of 6.5 percent or more, confirmed by a second abnormal result — but use glucose criteria when red-cell turnover makes HbA1c unreliable.

props.label: HbA1c unreliable when red-cell turnover changes

explanation.what: Plain language: diabetes means blood sugar stays too high; the lab shows it with a fasting sugar, a sugar after a sweet drink, or a long-term sugar marker on red cells. Scientific terms: ADA diagnostic criteria are FPG ≥ 126 mg/dL, 2-h plasma glucose ≥ 200 mg/dL during a 75-g OGTT, HbA1c ≥ 6.5%, or random plasma glucose ≥ 200 mg/dL with classic symptoms; prediabetes is FPG 100–125, 2-h 140–199 or HbA1c 5.7–6.4%.
explanation.why: Glucose binds hemoglobin non-enzymatically in proportion to its concentration over the red cell’s ~120-day life, so HbA1c reflects average glycemia over months. When red-cell age shifts (bleeding, transfusion, hemolysis) or in pregnancy, G6PD deficiency and HIV, HbA1c no longer tracks glucose. One result can be an error, so a second abnormal result is required unless hyperglycemia is unequivocal.
explanation.measure: Plasma glucose (fasting, OGTT, random) and HbA1c; for gestational diabetes, a one-step 75-g OGTT at 24–28 weeks with fasting ≥ 92, 1-h ≥ 180 or 2-h ≥ 153 mg/dL (any one). Fructosamine and glycated albumin are alternatives when HbA1c is unreliable for monitoring.
explanation.differs: Diagnosis (two abnormal results) vs screening; non-pregnant cut-offs vs gestational cut-offs (lower, any one value); HbA1c (months, red-cell dependent) vs plasma glucose (now).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: the three diagnostic cut-offs, prediabetes ranges, an HbA1c after transfusion or hemolysis (don’t use it), a random glucose without symptoms (not diagnostic), and GDM one-step values.

Used when HbA1c is unreliable and in GDM testing

comparisons.distinguisher: Whether the result depends on red-cell lifespan.

mnemonic.explanation: Fasting 126, 2-hour (or random with symptoms) 200, HbA1c 6.5%; in pregnancy the one-step OGTT uses 92, 180 and 153, and one value is enough.
mnemonic.limitation: HbA1c is unreliable when red-cell turnover changes, the random 200 rule needs symptoms, and outside pregnancy a second abnormal result is needed. Units are mg/dL; mmol/L values differ (126 mg/dL ≈ 7.0 mmol/L).

analogyLimitations: Ladders and doors are memory devices, not risk scales.
Glucose “tokens” sticking to a red cell exaggerate glycation for clarity.
The example results (131 mg/dL, 6.7%) are invented.
takeaway: Diabetes is diagnosed by a fasting glucose of 126 or more, a 2-hour OGTT of 200 or more, or an HbA1c of 6.5 percent or more, confirmed by a second abnormal result — but use glucose criteria when red-cell turnover makes HbA1c unreliable.

questions.stem: A non-pregnant adult without symptoms has a fasting plasma glucose of 131 mg/dL and, from the same sample, an HbA1c of 6.7%. What is the interpretation?

options.text: Diabetes — two abnormal results confirm the diagnosis
options.rationale: Correct. Both exceed diagnostic cut-offs (≥ 126 mg/dL and ≥ 6.5%); two abnormal results, even from one sample, confirm diabetes.
Incorrect. Prediabetes is FPG 100–125 or HbA1c 5.7–6.4%; both values are above those ranges.

options.text: Normal — only a random glucose can diagnose diabetes
options.rationale: Incorrect. Fasting glucose and HbA1c are standard diagnostic tests.

options.text: Needs a third test before any diagnosis
options.rationale: Incorrect. ADA requires two abnormal results; both are already present.

questions.stem: A patient who received two units of red cells last week has an HbA1c of 6.9%. What is the best next step for diagnosing diabetes?

options.text: Use plasma glucose criteria (fasting glucose or OGTT) instead of HbA1c
options.rationale: Correct. Transfusion changes red-cell age, so HbA1c no longer reflects average glucose.
Incorrect. The HbA1c is uninterpretable after transfusion.
Incorrect. A day later the transfused cells are still present; the problem persists.
Incorrect. Urine glucose is not a diagnostic criterion.

questions.stem: At 26 weeks of pregnancy, a one-step 75-g OGTT gives fasting 88, 1-hour 185 and 2-hour 140 mg/dL. What is the result?

options.rationale: Correct. In the one-step test, any one value at or above its cut-off (92, 180, 153) diagnoses GDM.

options.text: Normal — two values must be abnormal
options.rationale: Incorrect. The one-step criteria require only one abnormal value.

options.text: Normal — 185 is below the non-pregnant 200 cut-off
options.rationale: Incorrect. Pregnancy uses lower cut-offs; 200 is the non-pregnant 2-hour value.
Incorrect. These criteria diagnose gestational diabetes, not type 2 diabetes.

claims.text: Diabetes: FPG ≥ 126, 2-h OGTT ≥ 200, HbA1c ≥ 6.5%, or random ≥ 200 with classic symptoms; two abnormal results needed without unequivocal hyperglycemia.

HbA1c reflects glucose over the red-cell life span (~120 days); use plasma glucose in pregnancy, G6PD deficiency, HIV and conditions altering red-cell turnover; fructosamine and glycated albumin are alternatives.
One-step GDM: 75-g OGTT at 24–28 weeks; fasting ≥ 92, 1 h ≥ 180, 2 h ≥ 153 mg/dL; any one value diagnoses.
HbA1c reflects 2–4 months with about 50% from the prior month; fresh or young red cells lower HbA1c.
